messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Duc Tran, a 52-year-old HVAC technician, had been working in the field for nearly three decades when a routine service call changed everything. He was repairing an aging commercial unit in the basement of a small manufacturing plant when a corroded valve gave way, releasing a cloud of methylene chloride. Duc breathed it in before he could reach the door; the acrid sweetness hit his throat, then his chest tightened, and he spent the next two hours coughing in the ER. Medically he was cleared within days, but something inside him never cleared.

Months later, Duc could still feel that chemical burn at the back of his throat whenever he caught a whiff of solvent or entered a poorly ventilated space. He began turning down jobs in basements or tight mechanical rooms; he told his dispatcher he was getting too old for cramped work, but the real reason was a deep, unshakeable certainty that the air was unsafe. Even when the safety data sheet showed no risk, even when his supervisor assured him the equipment was sealed, Duc found it impossible to trust that he was safe. His body stayed braced—shoulders hunched, jaw tight, ready to flinch at the slightest change in air pressure or a new smell.

This constant sense of imminent danger drove Duc to strategies that made life more manageable but also more restricted. Because he could not trust that a quiet room was harmless, he avoided relaxing entirely: after work he would find chores—reorganizing his toolbox, checking the seals on his own home’s ducts—rather than sit still or lie down. The moment he tried to unwind, his mind would flash to the basement, to that chemical taste, and he would spring up again. Being alone in the house felt just as threatening; he believed that if something went wrong, no one would be there to help or to confirm the danger was real. So he stayed near his wife, María, or called his son just to hear another voice, even when he had nothing to say. He also began avoiding any potential stressor—social plans, doctor’s appointments, even the evening news—because any unexpected event might force him to confront a situation he could not control. His world narrowed to the most predictable routines: work, home, sleep, repeat.

The strategies created their own weight. Duc’s avoidance of relaxation and solitude meant he was always in motion or in someone’s company, but he never felt rested. His body stayed on alert; he checked the front door and back windows three times before bed each night, then again when he woke to use the bathroom, even though he lived in a quiet suburb with good locks. He told himself he was being cautious, but he knew it was more than that—it was a compulsion born of the conviction that danger could breach his walls at any moment.

What finally brought Duc to seek help was a breakdown at work. He was assigned a standard duct-cleaning job in a school gymnasium; when he walked in and smelled chlorine from the pool, he froze, broke into a cold sweat, and walked out without a word. His supervisor called him the next day, concerned. Duc sat in the kitchen with María and admitted he could not keep living this way. He was terrified that the next job would be impossible, that his body would betray him, that the world he used to move through easily had become a minefield. He hoped—though he barely let himself believe it—that talking to someone could teach him how to breathe again without first checking the air.
